utterances.text: The one on the left is the original death certificate that came together with the autopsy report for each bag labelled with a code that you can read on top, in this case PSII/18. As you can see, it is an official Serb death certificate, as much as I am acquainted with from my work there, written in Cyrillic. It has the name of the victim on the first -- on the first line, and then I presume is the date of death on the second line. The second one on the right is the translation of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What does the code PSII/18 stand for?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Petrovo Selo II, body 18.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We see that this document is signed by a Professor V. Otasevic, do you know who this person is?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, it's Professor Vujadin Otasevic from the forensic institute in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And while you were head of OMPF, did you have any dealings or contacts with Professor Otasevic?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, as a matter of fact the first eight bodies that were transferred were thanks to -- the -- I cannot find the right word to say, but the dealings we had with Professor Otasevic were quite collaborative I would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender this exhibit, this is 00213. There are a set of other similar exhibits -- similar death certificates and documents from this same institution which I'm not going to go through unless it assists Your Honours with the witness in detail. The exhibits are -- go from the range 002114 [sic] to 00226.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you suggesting this should be separate from them or part of that batch?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Each one of them has a separate exhibit number. I can call each exhibit number separately. They go from the range 00213 to 00226.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: For our purposes I'm asking one exhibit or --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Separate exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Separate exhibits. They will be received then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document currently on the screen, Your Honours, with 65 ter number 00213 would be P00457; 65 ter 00214 would be P00458; 65 ter number 00215 would be P00459; 65 ter number 00216 would be P00460; 65 ter number 00217 would be P00461; 65 ter number 00218 would be P00462; 65 ter number 00219 would be P00463; 65 ter number 00220 would be P00464; 65 ter number 00221 would be P00465; 65 ter number 00222 would be P00466; 65 ter number 00223 would be P00467; 65 ter number 00224 would be P00468; 65 ter number 00225 would be P00469; and 65 ter number 00226 would be P00470, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Witness, now turning to your report and to the conclusions that you reach in your report, in your report you refer to identifying and differentiating between different types of trauma in bone. In very simple terms can you explain, when you examine remains, bone -- skeletal remains in this case, as you were explaining, how were you able to distinguish between gun-shot trauma and other types of trauma?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Right. I will try to be as simple as possible, but please feel free to interrupt me if I use terms that may sound too complicated. Bones break because of different mechanisms, and different mechanisms are characterised primarily by the energy that is applied to bone. For example, blunt-force trauma on bone is a load applied slowly over a large area. For example, a rock thrown to somebody's head or somebody being beaten with a hammer or something of the kind. Why it's a slow load? Because the velocity involved in this is quite low. If I have to calculate the velocity that my arm, holding a hammer, will get upon swinging my arm over the head of somebody will be a few metres per second. On the other hand, all the types of trauma such as, for example, gun-shot trauma are considered high-velocity trauma, because unlike the previous example, a bullet leaving the muzzle of a weapon would have, at the very least -- I mean, the lowest possible calibre over a hundred metres per second. So it is exponentially much much higher than blunt-force. And also it acts upon a much smaller area of the body. A bullet may have, let's say, 9 millimetres in diameter while a hammer would have a few centimetres in diameter. Bones do react to external loads or forces in various ways. For example, all materials have what is called an elastic phase and a plastic phase, and then they break. I give you another example. Let's say we have a plastic pen. If I bend this plastic pen with both of my hands, I will deform it. So it will go beyond its elasticity and will be plastically deformed. When I try to bend it over and to have it straight again, I won't be able to; it will remain like that. Bones are the same. Bones can go through elastic phase. It will be an immature bone of a child. Children are very elastic, so to speak. Then it may go through the plastic deformation and then it will break. Typically blunt-force trauma will cause plastic deformation on bone, meaning the bone may break and may yield and stay like that; while gun-shot wound trauma would definitely perforate and destroy bone, make it break automatically. And all this is based on the amount of kinetic energy that is transferred from an object in movement to bone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in very lay-man terms, is the fragmentation observed on the bone different in the case of blunt-force trauma and gun-shot trauma?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Both -- in general terms both characteristics are mutually exclusive, so there is a number of details of stigmata of each of these types of mechanisms that are totally different from one other. In other words, yes, it is possible to distinguish what is blunt force and what is gun-shot.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how are you able to distinguish between trauma that is suffered by the bone before or at the time of death and that that is suffered after the time of death? For example, during the transport of bones from Serbia to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: In general --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all unnecessary microphones please be turned off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Right. Sorry. I don't know if it's for me or for somebody else. The trauma caused at the time of death or around the time of death that we shall call peri mortem - in latin peri, around; mortem, trauma - has some specific characteristics. But before I go into that, I will try to link this with the rest of the answer. By definition, all these bodies that were transported from Serbia back to Kosovo, since we knew that these bodies have been buried and then dug up and then taken and then reburied and then exhumed again, we have to assume that all blunt-force trauma found in those remains could have been caused by post mortem phenomenon. In other words, I could not have said, unless some very specific characteristics were found, that somebody was clubbed to death, for example, or that somebody -- or that that damage was actually caused by an excavator ripping through bodies. Now, regarding the last point that was actually in your question. The patterns of bone damage caused by, for example, mechanical means of excavation are very typical. They cause, for example, major crushing injuries over large parts of anatomical areas, like the chest, the head. It causes transverse fractures of long bones with no radiating fractures of any kind. These are very typical post-mortem changes caused by mechanical instruments, such as excavators and so on. I may add that we, regrettably, had a very large experience with this dealing primarily with the Srebrenica case in which these type of practices were very common. I do not know whether I answered your question or I went off of it too much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ

Are you able to clarify that now?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes -- actually, it would be very helpful if we would go back to page 12 with the original pictures we saw before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This would be page 35 on -- in e-court, if the exhibit is still one single exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may use the -- this pen again. Peri mortem trauma, such as in this case, a gun-shot wound to the head, is associated, depending on the mechanism that is causing it, to the dissipation of energy. This energy dissipates through fractures. We can see - and I'm going to try to do my best to point on this graph -- suddenly it went off focus. I don't know if it was me or -- we got that fracture there that is associated to this defect -- this elongated defect we are seeing. In other words, peri mortem trauma has a relationship between two things: Specific defects such as the one we observing there and dissipation of energy through fractures. These fractures run depending on what bone they are located through the areas of least resistance of bone. And if they cross areas that are heavily reinforced or protected or buttressed, as we say, it means that the energy that is being dissipated is quite high, such as in this case, for example, this area here is an area of a buttress, as an occipital buttress, and you can see that the fracture is running around it, not crossing it. Having said that, this area of the bone, the occipital bone, is very thick. In other words, this type of fracture is a peri mortem fracture because it is associated to a specific defect that can be identified or traced to a gun-shot wound.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So, Witness, here we have a graph that is included in your report which refers to the distribution of probable gun-shot injuries per anatomical area. Which conclusions, if any, can be drawn from this graph that you have included in your report?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes. Again, I'll try to be as succinct as I can. It is -- it has been learned now, over the last few years, looking at the distribution of injuries or death in war conditions - it could be Iraq or Afghanistan or the Balkans for that matter after the disintegration of Yugoslavia - that the first cause of mortality or morbidity, meaning people dying or being injured in a traditional conflict, armed conflict - by "tradition" I mean where two armed groups are fighting one another, it doesn't really matter whether they are regular or irregular - is shrapnel, meaning the leading cause of mortality and morbidity is shrapnel. The second cause is gun-shot, and there is a very important difference between these two because gun-fires are also known as weapons of volition. In other words, if I want to kill one person in a crowd, I would not throw a grenade that would certainly kill everybody including the person I'm trying to kill, while shrapnel primarily comes from sectorial weapons, I mean, a bomb that goes off, a mortar, a grenade, or something of the kind. When we look at the distribution of injuries of people injured by gun-fire, a pattern emerges. In traditional conflicts, as per the definition I gave, the distribution of gun-shot injuries should be, that is based on some 25 traditional conflicts that were examined as a matter of fact when I wrote this report and has been expanded further in some other publications: First the limbs, meaning legs and arms; second, the trunk; and third, the head. Whenever we're dealing with the opposite scenario, meaning when there is an armed group and another group that is not necessarily armed, meaning a non-confrontational or armed confrontational context, we tend to find the reverse, meaning the head first, the distribute of gun-shot injuries in this case, the head first; the trunk; and then the extremities. What we're looking at in this graph is that we have the head with 300 individuals; the trunk with 323, so they are very close; followed by the limbs. So this pattern is an anomalous pattern of what you expect to find in a traditional armed confrontation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you referred to shrapnel injury, and in your report you said that from the cases that you were able to examine you were only able to find three cases of individuals that had sustained shrapnel injury and one that had sustained both shrapnel and gun-shot wounds for the sites of Batajnica and Lake Perucac, and for Petrovo Selo you say that all individuals had ascertained gun-shot wounds. Which conclusions, if any, can be drawn from this fact that you state in your report?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That it is highly likely that the pattern being observed corresponds to a non-confrontational pattern of armed conflict. If I have this evidence to elaborate, I would say that it is highly unlikely, improbable in this case, that this distribution of injuries is consistent with the confrontation of two armed groups. As an example I would tell you that 0.5 per cent, meaning three individuals, in all sites combined, have shrapnel injuries and 0.1 per cent has shrapnel and bullet wounds. So it is a totally insignificant number compared to the proportions of people that sustained gun-shot wounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And can any conclusions be drawn based on this pattern that you were able to observe as to the circumstances of how these individuals met their death?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, if we look at yet again the distribution of injuries, it would be quite interesting to see that we got 300 people that sustained gun-shot wounds to the head, the head being a very restricted area or very discrete area of the body, certainly is not the area where you expect to have such a high number of injuries unless they were purposely inflicted in that area. What I'm saying is, if you're shooting, you're going to go for the bulk of the body for the largest area not for the smallest area, that in this case would be the head or a hand or a foot or something of the kind. The other important issue to be drawn from this is that the number of cases in which cause of death was not ascertained was primarily because of the destruction of these remains, meaning they were very fragmented or they were burned or they were incomplete. So this means that such a large number of cases with gun-shot wounds is defining as a context that the real number of people injured by a gun-shot is much higher than we're observing here. It has been proven, and there is a study of a Frenchman, another associate that is listed in my report, that the number of people that show skeletal injuries, bone injuries, in a fire-fight context is only a fraction of the people that actually were injured or died of gun-shot. For example, if you are shot through soft tissues of the abdomen, you will not find -- have a broken bone; if you are shot through the spine or the head, you will have a broken bone. But if -- let's say we have ten people that have been in a fire-fight of some kind, maybe three or four will show skeletal injuries, while the rest will not; but the rest also sustained gun-shot injuries although they have no broken bones.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you have referred several times to the fact that you examined mostly skeletal remains because there was very little soft tissue in the remains you examined. Was this is case for all three mass grave sites or was there a different for one or two of the sites?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, the site of Petrovo Selo, the PS, site consisted of primarily saponified or in some cases what we call wet, mummified tissues, meaning body fat was saturated in some cases giving the appearance to some waxy material, or bodies were slightly desecrated keeping some humidity as well in some areas and having recognisable muscle in pink colour. This actually means the examination of these remains was much easier, "easier," in as much we were dealing with cadavers. It was almost a proper corpse, so to speak, while the remains in Ba and D sites were primarily disarticulated bones.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I understand from your report that that was one of the sites where you found no cases of shrapnel injury; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What conclusion if any can be drawn from that?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That the under representation of shrapnel injuries is actually real. It is not, to say, an artefact of the examination. In other words, in the Petrovo Selo cases that I think were 60 -- 61 cases, yes, 61 cases, 53 of them showed gun-shot wounds and none showed shrapnel. We cannot say that we have missed shrapnel injuries in these remains because they were complete; and on top of it as any other remain all of them were gone through X-ray examination to look for any metal particles that can be lodged or found anywhere in the body. And since the soft tissues were there -- since they were there, you could see them. So what I'm trying to say is a low representation of shrapnel injuries in all the samples likely probably reflects what actually happened, meaning that very few people were injured by shrapnel; i.e., shrapnel was not the first means of injury or mechanism of injury that operated in these sites.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And with regard to the distribution of injuries per anatomical area, was the site of Petrovo Selo similar to that which we just saw for Lake Perucac and Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, in Petrovo Selo we have 20 individuals with injuries on the head and 21 on the chest, so it's almost the same with a difference of one. Upper limbs, there are five; and 13 on the lower limbs. So it would be in order: Chest, head, and limbs, but obviously head and chest are almost identical.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And going back to what we were talking about about the circumstances in which these individuals had met their death, can you make any specific or draw any specific conclusions with regard to this site of Petrovo Selo based on what you were able to observe?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, the conclusions regarding Petrovo Selo would not be different to the ones drawn for the other two sites with the exception that no shrapnel injuries were detected, meaning that the only type of weapons that were likely used were, I mean, guns of some -- fire-arms of some denomination. In this case, if I recall well, all injuries were caused by high-velocity rounds, meaning rounds fired likely by rifle of some kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to turn away from your report now, and I just have very few questions left with regard to the consolidated list of missing persons that is referred to in your statement at paragraph 31. You refer to this list and you indicate in your statement how it is compiled and you say it is updated at regular intervals. Do you know how regularly this list is updated since it was first created?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, obviously from my recollection I no longer work for MPF, the list was updated almost on a monthly basis. Primarily the issue with this list is that we wanted to have a list that could be accepted by all parties or former parties to the conflict. So this list was compared constantly with the International Committee of the Red Cross list, since obviously they are the neutral body by excellence, that have a similar list to ours; and the idea was to try to get to agreement to the two lists to see why cases that were in their list were not in ours and so forth. But certainly the list was constantly updated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In your statement you refer -- you indicated that you had provided to the ICTY two versions of this list, one from December of 2004 and one from October 2006. Have you recently had the chance to review a more updated list from April 2008?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And can you just very generally tell us what differences you were able to observe when you reviewed that list from the most recent one you had seen at the time of your statement, which is October 2006?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: The difference between the two lists is the last one from April 2008, the total number of cases is higher. So if in October 2006 we had a total universe of 5.298 cases, in April 2008 there were 5.367 cases. Equally, the number of cases closed and the number of cases active in both lists are obviously different. Why do we close cases? Primarily through a number of mechanisms. One of them could be that the person turns out to be alive; therefore, the name of this person has to be eliminated from the list. Actually what we do is we simply close the case, the name remains there as a record. Or we have to close a case and there is no information whatsoever regarding whether this person actually existed or the conditions in which this person went missing. Another reason for closing a case would be to identify the remains, what is what mostly happened, identifying the remains and returning them to the families. Or maybe identifying the remains and we have not yet broken the news to the families but the remains have been identified. So we know that Mr. John Doe has been identified, now has a name, and pending explaining to the family that we have identified their loved one, the remains in the list changed status to a closed case. And that is why, as of April 2008, there were 3.241 cases closed, all reasons combined; and there were 2.126 cases active, meaning whereabouts of missing persons still unknown.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that this April 2008 list now represents the most updated and exhaustive record of the missing persons reported missing during the Kosovo conflict?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I would say so, but I would also suspect, I do not know that because I have not been in contact with my former office, that there are other versions of that list as of January or February 2009, I do not know. But obviously April 2008 would be as exhaustive record as there was until April 2008, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: However, what I want to know is the exact name of the university where you pursued this course of studies, I believe that this was in 1994?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That was in 1991, University College London, part of University of London.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me your master's thesis. Did you have to write it? What was your topic, and who was your supervisor, if you did have to produce a thesis?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I could not tell you the title of it because it escapes me, but I can tell you a subject and tell you also whom my supervisor was. Starting with my supervisor, it was Professor Don Brothwell. I believe he is a professor of merit in the southern university of York these days, and I worked with an archaeological collection from the central coast of Peru dealing with trace element analysis for the reconstruction of diet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is that all?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question is this: Before you went to Great Britain, did you have any medical training?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As you did your master's thesis, did you take any courses in medicine; and if yes, could you please elaborate?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You note in your CV that for all intents and purposes you also did some work in heart science, such as, for instance, archaeology - just a moment, I do apologise -- that you actually combined archaeology, physical anthropology, and forensic medicine. And now you tell us that you didn't do any medical studies; however, this is what I read in your CV. And that's why I'm asking you: Why do you now tell us that you didn't do any forensic medicine studies, whereas in your CV this is what it says? Is that an error? Can I consider it to be an error?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Should be because I have mentioned as a matter of fact during the examination-in-chief that it was a combination between physical anthropology, bio-archaeology, and forensics. I never used the word "medicine."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned forensic medicine. What do you mean when you say "forensics"? What is it?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: "Forensics" is an ever-evolving field that contains a number of sub-disciplines of forensic medicine itself. It could be criminalistics, could be trace analysis, could be elements of forensic pathology, could be scene of crime reconstruction, could be, frankly, a number of things. And I reiterate the fact that I have mention the word "forensics" in that open and wide spectrum of disciplines.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is why I asked you this, and this is why I want you to tell us whether you meant forensics in the broadest sense or whether you meant only one segment of this science that you studied in London?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, I tell you again that I dealt with forensics, meaning all the aspects of forensic sciences as applied to the examination of skeletal remains, be they found in an archaeological context or in a medical or legal context.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me now whether you ever studied human anatomy - and here I mean the overall anatomy - or did you just study human skeletons?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I have not had any formal education on human anatomy in the way you describe it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you focus in particular on human skeleton?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: During my education, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When and where? You said that you did it in the course of your studies, and I want to ask you: When and where? In what segment of your education?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: During the time I studied my B.A. in archaeology, there were two compulsory courses taught by the Faculty of Biology that were called physical anthropology, where you have to actually study skeletal anatomy as part of the courses. During my master's, I did a refreshment course on skeletal anatomy as part of my education, obviously, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, are you familiar with the basic tenets of pathophysiology and pathology?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, the basic tenets, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any formal education or is this something that you did in the course of your general education? So when you say that you have some knowledge of pathophysiology and pathology, did you take some exams, do you have some proof of that, or is this some knowledge that you gained as you went along in the course of your education?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: It is rather knowledge I gained during the course of my work, not during my education.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you came to Kosovo and Metohija as the head of the service where you remained until May 2007, did you take part in any forensic medical expert analyses of cases involving violent deaths before courts in your country or before any other courts before your arrival in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, I did, both in my countries, in this Tribunal, and as a member - and even in some cases - directing commissions of inquiry, could be for the UN or for any other body.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: While you worked here at the Tribunal, would you please tell me what jobs did you have, what posts, and what was it that you actually did?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Certainly. My first employment with the Tribunal was with the Rwanda Tribunal back in 1996, if I'm not mistaken it would be February 1996. My function or title then was forensic investigator. My work was as a forensic anthropologist for the Office of the Prosecutor, exhuming, analysing the remains found in mass graves following the genocide in Rwanda. I then was transferred on loan together with my unit to ICTY about June - if I'm not mistaken - June 1996, where I participated both in the exhumations of mass graves related to Srebrenica massacre as well as to the killings at the Ovcara farm in Croatia. In 1997 I was officially employed by ICTY, since at that time I was still technically employed by ICTR, as a forensic anthropologist; that was my functional title. Since then on I became the person responsible for setting up the teams that worked in the field and/or in the mortuary for the Tribunal and I -- my position was quite exchangeable. I could be an archaeologist dealing with exhumations of mass grave sites or chief anthropologist at the mortuary, until the year 2001, if I'm not mistaken, that is the last major operation of this Tribunal in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question: When you say that you worked as a forensic investigator for the ICTR, and later on for the ICTY too, do you mean that you actually worked as an OTP investigator?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, my functional title of forensic investigator was with ICTR, and I was appointed to the Office of the Prosecutor as a forensic person. I was not carrying out investigations -- criminal investigations, if you wish. But yes, I was appointed to the Office of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question: Most of the abduction reports of the team that you headed are signed by forensic medicine specialist doctor -- doctors, Dr. Marek Gasior --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, we could not get the names of the three doctors.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will have to repeat the names because I can see that they're not in the transcript -- [In English] Some problem with the microphone definitely. [Interpretation] Let me repeat the names, Marek Gasior, Asoka Senevirante [phoen], Ananda Samarasekera [phoen]. Am I right when I say that?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, there's a minor pronunciation or spelling issue, but yes, it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you will not take it amiss because I'm not really familiar with those names, but we understand each other and that's the point. So I go on to my next question. In various documents that follow, documents that have been admitted into evidence by the Trial Chamber, they were tendered by the Prosecution. They contain names of your colleagues, forensic anthropologists. And I would like to know whether there are CVs for all those people; in other words, their expertise, something that should be there before you even take them on to be on your team?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Certainly all the people which names appear in those documents would have a CV on file in my former office. I mean, obviously as a UN procedure, people were not employed without knowing who they were or what they have done. So I would definitely invite you to request those CVs if this is the case. I presume the CVs exist still. They were when I was head of the office, so I guess they would still exist now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Of course. I assumed that this was the case, but I have to ask you this because of my follow-up question. You, as the head of this section and the head of the whole team, were you the person who actually decided who you would work with? Did you decide whom to employ on the basis of their qualifications that were made known in accordance with the Rules of the United Nations or was it somebody else's decision?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No, I -- as a head, I had prerogatives certainly to employ certain people depending on what -- on how these people were employed. So let me clarify: If people were employed or as part of the UN on a UN contract, certainly, as you may know, the UN has very specific rules regarding hiring people. You have to short-list from an open-application process. There may be two people from your office and a third person from another office that is not yours and things of the kind, a number of interviews and so on. If people are employed, for example, on a short-term contract on another fund be, for example, on a donor fund, we had a number of donor funds, the process of recruiting is slightly more flexible. People maybe come for a month or even two weeks. In the case of pathologists, they came for a short time. In that case, yes, I had extensive leverage as to who I would hire. But certainly it was not me myself who was hand-picking every single expert. Certainly I gave an approving look or non-approving look at the CVs I received in order not to have people that were literally unqualified, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My question is: How great was your role in the selection of personnel, either full-time personnel or those who only worked on short-term contracts?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, it was the -- I mean, it was a rule that the head of an office dealing with what we deal has. I mean -- I mean, I -- it's a bit difficult for me to specify or quantify my role. I was a head of an office with a very important mandate in hand; therefore, I would definitely oversee things as much as I could, certainly. I mean, obviously delegating authority and all the rest of it, but obviously the issue was not that people would be employed, so to speak, without me knowing who they were primarily to deal with such a sensitive issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any cases where you decided that some people could no longer be on your team to do some jobs that they had done previously on the team?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Could you elaborate on that because I do not understand very much your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you fire anyone from your team, either somebody who was there like a full-time employee, a staff member, or on a short-term contract?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Instances of firing people primarily if they were on posts of any kind had to be decided by a committee, of which, as a matter of fact, I was not part of, in order to guarantee the rights of the person and investigation or whatever it may be. In cases of people working in short contracts, people in theory could be, yes, I mean fired upon finding some major breaches in their behaviour or work; and this could be a prerogative of mine as head of the office, yes, that is correct. However, I do not recall "firing" any person on this last category, meaning these short-term employees. However, I do recall an instance in which some of the staff members were "fired" through a very lengthy process with the Department of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question: I understand what you say about short-term contracts. You mentioned people who were on posts. You also mentioned the committee that was set up to protect all the rights of the employees, people who work there. And my question is: Could you recommend to such a committee that a person be -- that a person's employment be terminated for a serious breach of duty or any kind of criminal behaviour? Did you have this opportunity -- did you have this prerogative?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, I did. As head of the office, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My last question in this line of questioning is: In percentages, how many people were on short-term contracts and how many people were staff members? Could you please answer and then I have a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That is a very difficult question to answer based on recollections -- but again, based on recollections and stating really that it is only a recollection, the number of people -- of experts on short-term contracts depended on the workload we had. In other words, I give you an example. Imagine that we had a transfer of remains from Serbia proper into Kosovo of a hundred bodies. Obviously as soon as these bodies or body-bags crossed the Inter-Entity Boundary Line, the families were pressing us to return these bodies to them, so we needed to work fast. So in that case we would hire a number of people to work, for example, for two weeks in the mortuary and to finish with that back-load of cases. But then maybe there would be no transfer until, who knows when, a few months ahead, and the exhumations being conducted in Kosovo would yield a few bodies that could be actually dealt with by the permanent staff we had in the office. So the extra personnel, meaning these short-term personnel, will go home and we will remain with the people we had. If I had to give you a precise number of permanent posts, I mean from my recollection maybe we were -- on UN posts maybe there were 15 and there were a number of other people on KCB, Kosovo Consolidated Budget posts, at the time -- or there was a time in which the office they were primarily staffed by KCB staff. We were, like, 79 or 80-something people. If we add to this the short-termers, the short-termers could be up to 10 people or 12 people, so you can have an idea of how many people were working at the same time in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Mr. Djordjevic, I've got to interrupt with time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I wanted to take this opportunity after the witness responded to tell you that my next question would require a five-minute answer, so I wanted to concur with you this is the right time to make a break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We must adjourn for the evening now, to resume tomorrow in the morning, and the court officer will show you out and give you instructions, and we look forward to continuing with your evidence tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While the witness is leaving, Ms. Kravetz, I understand there is a matter you wish to raise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. It's a matter that concerns scheduling. The witness who's scheduled to testify right after we conclude with this witness is Mr. Jan Kickert. The witness is already here, he has arrived to The Hague, and he has informed us today that he needs to return home tomorrow at the end of the day to attend some personal matters. We would like to request to start tomorrow first thing with Mr. Kickert's testimony and complete his evidence and later continue with Mr. Baraybar's testimony. That is, to interrupt Mr. Baraybar's testimony right now. I should point out that I had informed my learned colleagues from the Defence about the fact that Mr. Kickert had to complete his evidence tomorrow at the start of the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Have you consulted with the present witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: He has no problem staying if his testimony goes over the weekend and needs to continue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How long do you expect Mr. Kickert will take in total tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Well, in direct he will take approximately one hour. I don't know how much time the Defence anticipates to take in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, do you anticipate difficulty in finishing the evidence of Mr. Kickert tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we proceed as my colleague, Ms. Kravetz, suggested, I don't see any problems; but life has taught us that there may be all kinds of problems. So with this caveat, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Life has taught this Chamber that whatever time in estimates is bound to be inadequate, a matter about which we are gradually effecting change in the approach of counsel on both sides. Thank you for that. We look forward to the evidence of Mr. Kickert first up tomorrow and we will then progress later in the morning to the evidence of the present witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We adjourn now to resume tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 20th day of March, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.04 p.m.,
